items.stem: In the linear model y = Xβ + u, y is 50×1 and X is 50×5 (the first column of X is the intercept). If R² = 0.55, the adjusted R² is (to three decimals)
items.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k), where k counts every column of X, the intercept included. Here 1 − (1 − 0.55) × 49/45 = 0.510. Trap: using n − k − 1 counts the intercept twice and gives 0.499.

items.stem: Consider the two-equation model (i) y₁ = γ₁y₂ + β₁₁ x₁ + β₁₂ x₂ + ε₁ and (ii) y₂ = γ₂y₁ + β₂₂ x₂ + ε₂, where the y's are endogenous and the x's are exogenous (all coefficients shown are non-zero). Then
items.explanation: With G = 2 equations, an equation is identified when it excludes at least G − 1 = 1 exogenous variable that appears elsewhere in the system (order condition; with two equations and non-zero coefficients this also satisfies the rank condition). (i) excludes no exogenous variable and (ii) excludes x₁, so: (ii) is identified but (i) is not. Trap: including more exogenous variables in an equation makes it harder, not easier, to identify.

items.explanation: With G = 2 equations, an equation is identified when it excludes at least G − 1 = 1 exogenous variable that appears elsewhere in the system (order condition; with two equations and non-zero coefficients this also satisfies the rank condition). items.stem: In the regression model y = Xβ + u with two regressors, X′X = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] and E(X′u) = δ = (1, 2)′ (X fixed). If b = (X′X)⁻¹X′y is the OLS estimator, then E(b − β) is
items.explanation: b − β = (X′X)⁻¹X′u, so E(b − β) = (X′X)⁻¹E(X′u) = (X′X)⁻¹δ. Here (X′X)⁻¹ = [[1, −1], [−1, 2]] (determinant 1), and multiplying by δ gives (−1, 3)′. OLS is unbiased only when E(X′u) = 0. Trap: (X′X)δ multiplies instead of solving, and δ alone forgets (X′X)⁻¹.

items.stem: The true model is y = β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + u with β₁ = 2, β₂ = 3 and E(u) = 0 (no intercept; x₁, x₂ fixed with Σx₁² = 10, Σx₁x₂ = 4, Σx₂² = 8). If y is regressed on x₁ alone, b₁ = Σx₁y/Σx₁² has expectation
items.explanation: Substituting the true model: b₁ = Σx₁(β₁x₁ + β₂x₂ + u)/Σx₁² = β₁ + β₂Σx₁x₂/Σx₁² + Σx₁u/Σx₁². Taking expectations, E(b₁) = 2 + 3 × 4/10 = 16/5. This is omitted-variable bias: it vanishes only if β₂ = 0 or x₁ and x₂ are orthogonal. Trap: dividing by Σx₂² regresses x₁ on x₂ instead of x₂ on x₁.
